---
title: "Spatial networks with sf"
description: >
  Networks whose nodes and edges are simple features: building them from
  sf tables, lines, and polygons, measuring along geometry, keeping the
  network consistent through spatial operations, drawing maps, and
  exchanging data with sfnetworks and GeoPackage files.
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
has_sf <- requireNamespace("sf", quietly = TRUE)
has_sfnetworks <- has_sf && requireNamespace("sfnetworks", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = has_sf,
                      fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5)
```

A spatial network is a network whose nodes, edges, or both have a place.
In knappnet that place is carried by the [sf](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/)
package: the node table, the edge table, or both are simple-feature data
frames, with any geometry type and a coordinate reference system. Nothing
else changes. The network is still two data frames, connectivity still
comes from the `from` and `to` columns, and every measure runs exactly as
it does on a plain network. The geometry is there for what geometry is good
for: lengths, neighbourhoods, filters, joins, and maps.

The division of labour is strict. sf (with GEOS and s2 underneath) does
all the geometry; the engine never sees a coordinate it did not ask for.
What crosses from one side to the other are numbers: edge lengths that
become distance weights, and one representative point per node that the
point-based functions of `net_spatial()` use. sf is a suggested
package: knappnet installs and works without it, and every function on this
page says so clearly if it is missing.

```{r setup, eval = TRUE}
library(knappnet)
```

```{r, eval = !has_sf, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat("*The sf package is not installed where this page was built, so the",
    "code below is shown but not run.*\n")
```

## Nodes and edges as simple features

Any sf data frame can be the node table. Here four weather stations in UTM
zone 33N (coordinates in metres) are joined by three links:

```{r}
stations <- sf::st_as_sf(
  data.frame(name = c("north", "east", "south", "west"),
             x = c(500000, 503000, 500000, 497000),
             y = c(6003000, 6000000, 5997000, 6000000),
             elevation = c(120, 85, 90, 140)),
  coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32633)
links <- data.frame(source = c("north", "east", "south"),
                    target = c("east", "south", "west"))
g <- net_frame(links, stations, directed = FALSE)
g
```

`net_frame()` noticed the sf table on its own. The geometry column and the
CRS are recorded as roles next to the identifier and endpoint columns, and
the node table is kept exactly as it was given, geometry included:

```{r}
g$roles[c("id", "node_geometry", "edge_geometry")]
g$roles$crs$Name
g$nodes
```

Edges may have geometry too. `net_to_sf()` returns either table as sf; for
edges without geometry it draws straight lines between the endpoints,
which sfnetworks calls *spatially implicit* edges. Giving those lines back
to `net_frame()` makes them explicit, and the two tables must then agree on
the CRS (an error with the fix explains if they do not):

```{r}
edge_lines <- net_to_sf(g, "edges")
edge_lines
h <- net_frame(edge_lines, stations, directed = FALSE)
h
```

Measures do not care which kind of network they get. The engine sees the
same three edges either way:

```{r}
net_degree(h)
net_betweenness(h)
```

## Lengths along the geometry

`net_edge_lengths()` is the bridge between geometry and weights. Without edge
geometry it measures between the nodes' points (great-circle distances for
longitude and latitude, Euclidean otherwise, as `net_spatial()`
documents). With edge geometry it defers to `sf::st_length()`, which is
geodesic for longitude and latitude and planar in the units of a projected
CRS, and it records the unit:

```{r}
net_edge_lengths(g)
net_edge_lengths(h)
```

A bent edge is longer than the straight one between the same nodes, and
an edge whose geometry is empty falls back to the straight distance, so a
table where only some edges have been digitized still has a length for
every row:

```{r}
bend <- sf::st_linestring(rbind(c(500000, 6003000), c(503000, 6003000), c(503000, 6000000)))
sf::st_geometry(edge_lines)[1] <- sf::st_sfc(bend, crs = 32633)
sf::st_geometry(edge_lines)[3] <- sf::st_sfc(sf::st_linestring(), crs = 32633)
mixed <- net_frame(edge_lines, stations, directed = FALSE)
mixed
net_edge_lengths(mixed)
```

Lengths become weights in the usual way, and path-based measures then
follow travel distance rather than hop count:

```{r}
mixed$edges$metres <- as.vector(net_edge_lengths(mixed))
w <- net_frame(mixed$edges, stations, directed = FALSE, weight = "metres", weight_type = "distance")
net_distances(w)
```

## Representative points

Nodes need not be points. Regions, buildings, or river reaches can be
nodes, and the point-based functions reduce each geometry to one
representative point. By default that is `sf::st_point_on_surface()`,
which always lies on the geometry; `net_spatial(x, representative =
"centroid")` switches to `sf::st_centroid()`, which can fall outside a
concave shape. Here four unit squares form a 2-by-2 grid, and the group
geometry of the top and bottom rows is computed from the squares' points:

```{r}
square <- function(x, y) {
  sf::st_polygon(list(rbind(c(x, y), c(x + 1, y), c(x + 1, y + 1), c(x, y + 1), c(x, y))))
}
regions <- sf::st_sf(region = c("sw", "se", "nw", "ne"),
                     row = c("bottom", "bottom", "top", "top"),
                     geometry = sf::st_sfc(square(0, 0), square(1, 0), square(0, 1), square(1, 1),
                                           crs = 32633))
r <- net_from_polygons(regions, id = "region")
net_group_geometry(r, "row")
```

## Building networks from geometry

Two constructions come up constantly in spatial analysis, and both are
built in.

### Contiguity of regions

`net_from_polygons()` joins polygons that share a boundary. Under *queen*
contiguity a shared corner is enough; under *rook* contiguity the shared
boundary must be a line, as the chess pieces move. The relations are
evaluated exactly with `sf::st_relate()` and the DE-9IM patterns that
define them, which is also what `spdep::poly2nb()` does with `snap = 0`:

```{r}
net_from_polygons(regions, id = "region")$edges
net_from_polygons(regions, contiguity = "rook", id = "region")$edges
```

The edges of a contiguity network have no geometry of their own, so
`net_edge_lengths()` measures between the regions' representative points.

### Streets, rivers, and pipelines

`net_from_lines()` turns LINESTRING features into a network: each line is an
edge, and its endpoints are nodes shared with every other line ending at
the same place. With `tolerance = 0` endpoints must coincide exactly, as in
sfnetworks; a positive tolerance merges endpoints within that distance
(and, transitively, chains of them), which absorbs the small gaps that
digitized data often have. The lines keep every attribute and gain a
`length` column that becomes the network's distance weight. A small grid of
streets:

```{r}
segment <- function(x0, y0, x1, y1) sf::st_linestring(rbind(c(x0, y0), c(x1, y1)))
streets <- sf::st_sf(
  name = c("1st Ave", "2nd Ave", "3rd Ave", "A St", "B St", "C St"),
  geometry = sf::st_sfc(segment(0, 0, 200, 0), segment(0, 100, 200, 100), segment(0, 200, 200, 200),
                        segment(0, 0, 0, 200), segment(100, 0, 100, 200), segment(200, 0, 200, 200),
                        crs = 32633))
roads <- net_from_lines(streets)
roads
roads$edges
```

Each whole street is one edge here, so streets that cross without a vertex
at the crossing are not connected: the network knows the data, not the
map. `sf::st_intersection()` or `lwgeom::st_split()` can split the lines
at their crossings first when that is what the data mean. Once built, the
network is an ordinary net_frame, and shortest paths follow street length:

```{r}
net_distances(roads)[1, ]
```

### Proximity

`net_proximity()` accepts sf tables of any geometry. By default it
works from representative points through the engine's k-d tree; with
`exact = TRUE` it uses `sf::st_distance()` between the geometries
themselves, so two polygons that touch are at distance 0:

```{r}
net_proximity(regions, within = 1, id = "region")$edges
net_proximity(regions, within = 0, id = "region", exact = TRUE)$edges
```

## Spatial operations that keep the network consistent

Subsetting the node table by hand would break the edge index, so the
spatial operations come as functions that rebuild what they must.
`net_spatial_filter()` keeps the nodes whose geometry satisfies a predicate
with some features and returns the induced subnetwork; `net_spatial_join()`
attaches attributes of the features each node falls in; and
`net_transform()` reprojects both tables at once:

```{r}
inner <- sf::st_bbox(c(xmin = 498000, ymin = 5998000, xmax = 504000, ymax = 6004000),
                     crs = sf::st_crs(32633))
net_spatial_filter(h, inner)$nodes$name

zones <- sf::st_sf(zone = c("uptown", "downtown"),
                   geometry = sf::st_sfc(
                     sf::st_polygon(list(rbind(c(495000, 6001500), c(505000, 6001500),
                                               c(505000, 6005000), c(495000, 6005000),
                                               c(495000, 6001500)))),
                     sf::st_polygon(list(rbind(c(495000, 5995000), c(505000, 5995000),
                                               c(505000, 6001500), c(495000, 6001500),
                                               c(495000, 5995000))))),
                   crs = 32633)
net_spatial_join(h, zones)$nodes[, c("name", "zone")]

ll <- net_transform(h, 4326)
ll$roles$crs$Name
net_edge_lengths(ll)
```

The last line shows the geodesic lengths of the reprojected lines; they
differ from the planar UTM lengths by the projection's scale distortion,
a fraction of a percent here.

`net_check_geometry()` is the optional consistency check: does each edge
geometry start and end at (or within a tolerance of) its nodes? knappnet
never requires it, because connectivity comes from the endpoint columns,
but it is the first thing to run on data assembled from several sources:

```{r}
net_check_geometry(h)
net_check_geometry(mixed)
```

## Maps

`net_plot_spatial()` draws a spatial network at its true locations. Polygons
are filled with the node color, lines drawn in it, points drawn as points,
and edges follow their own geometry when they have one. Only base graphics
and sf's own plot methods are involved, colors come from palettes that are
safe for color-blind readers, and the usual appearance arguments work:

```{r}
net_plot_spatial(r, node_color = "row", main = "Queen contiguity of four regions")
net_plot_spatial(roads, node_label = FALSE, edge_color = "length", main = "Six streets")
net_plot_spatial(mixed, edge_width = 2, main = "Stations, with one bent and one implicit edge")
```

`plot()` on the same network draws an abstract layout, as for any other
net_frame. `net_plot_edge_lengths()` shows the distribution of edge lengths and,
given a `scale`, the `net_distance_decay()` curve it would imply, which is the
quickest way to pick a scale for distance-weighted ties:

```{r}
net_plot_edge_lengths(mixed, scale = 3000)
```

## Files and other packages

A spatial network can be written to, and read from, a GeoPackage, the
open standard that QGIS, GDAL, and sf all speak. The nodes and edges are
two layers (either may be an attribute table without geometry), and a
small third layer records the direction and the column roles so the
network reads back as it was written:

```{r}
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".gpkg")
net_write(roads, path)
sf::st_layers(path)$name
back <- net_read(path)
identical(net_distances(back), net_distances(roads))
unlink(path)
```

[sfnetworks](https://luukvdmeer.github.io/sfnetworks/) is the tidyverse
package for geospatial networks. Converting in either direction keeps
attributes and geometry; node identifiers travel as the `name` column that
igraph and tidygraph use:

```{r, eval = has_sfnetworks}
net <- net_to_sfnetwork(roads)
net
as_net_frame(net)
```

`sfnetworks::as_sfnetwork()` on a net_frame and `sf::st_as_sf()` on a
net_frame work as well.

## The planned Python mirror

The same design carries over to the Python package without translation.
A node or edge table there is a GeoPandas `GeoDataFrame`, which is a
pandas data frame with a geometry column and a CRS, just as an sf object
is a data frame with an sfc column. The convention of a pair of
GeoDataFrames, one for nodes and one for edges, is the one OSMnx
established with `graph_to_gdfs()` and `graph_from_gdfs()` (Boeing 2017),
so street networks downloaded with OSMnx will drop straight into the
Python net_frame. Geometry stays with GeoPandas and shapely (GEOS) and
pyproj; the engine receives lengths and representative points exactly as
it does from R, so every measure validated here is validated there.
